An increasing number of studies have recently documented the cholesterol paradox: patients with or at risk of heart failure (HF) often have unexpectedly low levels of LDL-C despite leading to cardiovascular diseases. This paper examines how well retrospective lipid panel measurements, supplemented with apolipoprotein B (ApoB), can predict an initial heart failure (HF) event in several pre-diagnosis time windows, using age-matched patient data from Electronic Health Records (EHRs). This retrospective study uses lipid profiles from multicenter nationwide EHRs from the All of Us Research Program. We apply machine learning and explainable AI (SHAP) to lipid-based prediction and to interpret cholesterol contributions to the diagnosis of first heart failure (HF). One experiment predicts the diagnosis of HF in 36 months; the other distinguishes HF patients from people who have never been diagnosed with cardiovascular disease. A baseline lipid panel that includes ApoB predicts the first HF event up to 36 months in advance, achieving an AUC of 0.624 in men and 0.627 in women. Compared to a group of the same age without previous cardiovascular disease, a lipid profile including ApoB predicts a first HF event with a substantially higher AUC: 0.937 for men and 0.925 for women. Shapley value analyses suggest that higher triglycerides and lower HDL and LDL levels are linked to subsequent HF events, with LDL appearing as the strongest yet counterintuitive predictor. ApoB ranks second in importance; in males, higher ApoB is associated with a greater risk of HF, unlike LDL. In general, the study highlights an unexpected association with LDL and emphasizes the prognostic utility of sex-specific metabolic indicators (TG, HDL) for HF using routinely collected clinical data.

items.title: Would an LLM Match into a Residency? Uncertainty, Reasoning and Image Use of Open Language Models on the Spanish MIR Examination
items.abstract_or_text: Accuracy on medical examinations is common evidence offered for the clinical use of language models, yet a health system that intends to run an open model on its own hardware needs to know considerably more: whether the model recognizes when it is likely to be wrong, whether medical fine-tuning improves this ability, whether its correct answers rest on sound clinical reasoning, or whether it actually uses the images it is given. We examine these questions for four open models of 8 to 27 billion parameters on the Spanish MIR residency examination, scoring 1,552 questions from eight editions under the exam's own rules. Answering every question, the three larger models would rank among roughly the first 600 to 3,000 candidates, with 41 to 43 specialties still open to them. Abstention, however, never pays, because even their least confident answers are right more often than the 25% break-even. Medical fine-tuning reduced overconfidence at the cost of accuracy, without improving how well confidence separates right from wrong answers. Moreover, 13-38% of correct answers rejected a distractor for a clinically unsound reason that confidence did not reflect, and removing or swapping the provided contextual images left accuracy unchanged.

items.title: RIPPLE: Recovery Internalization through Process-Level Policy Learning and Effect-Aware Credit for Long-Horizon Agentic Coding
items.abstract_or_text: Long-horizon coding agents can observe a failure and generate a plausible critique yet continue along the same incorrect trajectory. We call this the Critique-to-Action Handoff Gap. We introduce RIPPLE, a recovery-oriented training framework that internalizes process-level guidance into a single self-recovering policy. A prefix-only teacher provides evidence-grounded recovery supervision without access to future actions or terminal outcomes. After lightweight distillation, reinforcement learning assigns stage-specific credit to reflection triggering, diagnosis, and corrective action. Local validity signals gate trajectory advantages so that intermediate recovery decisions do not indiscriminately inherit terminal outcomes. Across four repository-level software-engineering benchmarks, RIPPLE improves the base policy by an arithmetic mean of 4.8 score points, with no auxiliary critic at deployment. Controlled ablations isolate the benefits of local, stage-aligned credit, and matched-prefix interventions show that critique semantics affect subsequent correction. Recovery gains concentrate where the prefix contains sufficient diagnostic evidence and the repository state remains reversible within the remaining budget.

items.title: Governance-State Corruption in Long-Term Memory for LLM Agents: A Cross-Model Stress Test
items.abstract_or_text: An LLM agent can retrieve a memory correctly yet use it incorrectly after its validity state changes. We study governance-state corruption: faults that alter which retained records enter model-visible context while stored content and tasks remain fixed. Across six providers, 731 benchmark-grounded bases yield 2,080 matched fault pairs. In offline control-plane checks, corruption changes the operative projection in 96.25% of pairs, while oracle-backed enforcement restores it in 100%. For downstream evaluation, a deterministically selected, non-probability LongMemEval/Memora panel resolves 298 of 300 matched triplets (238 distinct bases). Clean-minus-corrupted contrasts are 40.54 percentage points in LongMemEval binary correctness (95% base-cluster interval [30.32, 50.71]) and 30.60 points in rescaled Memora FAMA ([23.31, 37.69]); both sources also show recovery. OAKS Novel native option parity holds for all 6,714 resolved outputs. Full-cohort frozen-scorer corruption/recovery effects (-27.55/+27.51 points) remain descriptive proxies, not validated native semantic population effects. These bounded findings motivate evaluating memory control-state integrity alongside retrieval accuracy.

items.title: Mouse Neural Organoids Model the Mature In Vivo Synaptic Proteome
items.abstract_or_text: Neural organoids represent a promising approach for modelling neural circuits and neurological disease, yet their utility depends on whether they can recapitulate the molecular complexity of mature brain synapses. Here, we optimized a protocol to generate mature forebrain organoids from mouse embryonic stem cells and used time-resolved proteomics to define the emergence of synaptic proteins during maturation. Using fluorescence-activated synaptosome sorting coupled with mass spectrometry, we quantified the synapse-enriched proteome and found a high correlation with matched in vivo synaptic proteomes. These findings demonstrate that complex mature synaptic molecular architecture is present within an in vitro organoid environment.

items.title: Active Learning framework for Antibody Binding Affinity Prediction
items.abstract_or_text: Antibody engineering campaigns must prioritise variants from large combinatorial libraries under limited assay budgets. We present a Gaussian process (GP) active-learning benchmark for antibody-antigen binding affinity prediction across eight public AbBiBench assays spanning influenza hemagglutinin antibodies CR6261 and CR9114 and AAYL-series scFv libraries against the SARS-CoV-2 Spike HR2 peptide. The framework embeds variable heavy and light (VH/VL) sequences with ESM-2 650M, trains GP surrogates over compressed protein-language-model representations, and evaluates kernel, acquisition, representation, classical featurisation, and labelling-budget choices under a unified budget of 10\% of each full pool with a label-blind seed and a fixed held-out evaluation split. Across the benchmark, Tanimoto+UCB has the highest mean Recall@2\% point estimate among tested kernel-acquisition configurations, achieving 57.8\% mean Recall@2\% across five random seeds (68.3\% when scored against the acquisition-eligible pool), compared with 9.6\% for random selection -- a gap that is significant by a paired Wilcoxon test across datasets (p=0.0078); its point estimate is not significantly different from RQ+UCB or Tanimoto+EI at five seeds. We adopt the continuous Tanimoto kernel of gessner2024. The same configuration recovers the largest fractions of top binders in the influenza libraries (74.2\% on 3gbn\_h1, 82.7\% on 3gbn\_h9, and 84.9\% on 4fqi\_h3) while exposing harder AAYL combinatorial landscapes where recall remains lower and more variable. An additional three-seed representation ablation, run under the original protocol and not repeated after the evaluation corrections, ranked ESM-2 650M highest (mean Recall@2\% 0.673 \pm 0.28) among ProtBert, AntiBERTy, AbLang2, ProGen2, and classical encodings. On BindingGYM, the same configuration matches or exceeds ALLM-Ab on two of three datasets using the 100-sample held-out test metric. Structure-mapped Integrated Gradients and KernelSHAP analyses recover CDR-region attribution patterns consistent with contact-derived paratope geometry, though threshold-free (AUROC) analysis shows this qualitative agreement is not matched by strong residue-level discrimination. These results support Tanimoto-kernel GP active learning as a simple, reproducible strategy for label-efficient antibody affinity optimisation with qualitative structural validation.

items.title: An Interpretable Machine Learning Framework for Early- versus Late-Stage Classification of Breast Cancer from Gene Expression, with Co-expression Network Analysis
items.abstract_or_text: Anatomical stage is a principal determinant of treatment and prognosis in breast cancer, yet it is unclear how much information about stage is carried by the transcriptome of the primary tumour. We asked whether an a priori panel of 65 cancer-related genes can distinguish early-stage (AJCC Stage I-II) from late-stage (Stage III-IV) breast cancer, and which genes contribute to any signal. RNA-seq expression and pathologic stage for The Cancer Genome Atlas breast invasive carcinoma cohort (TCGA-BRCA) were obtained from the UCSC Xena platform. After restricting the data to primary tumours with a known stage, 1,075 tumours were analysed (805 early, 270 late) and split into stratified training (n = 860) and held-out test (n = 215) sets. Logistic regression, a support vector machine, random forest and gradient boosting were tuned by stratified five-fold cross-validation, with median imputation, standardisation and SMOTE oversampling fitted on training data only and classification thresholds chosen on out-of-fold training predictions. On the test set, Logistic Regression had the highest ROC-AUC, 0.618 (95% CI 0.530-0.704), with balanced accuracy 0.578, sensitivity 0.741 and specificity 0.416; differences in AUC between models were not statistically significant (DeLong p = 0.199-0.585). Permutation importance in the Gradient Boosting model ranked POU5F1, FLT3 and NOTCH1 highest, but this model's AUC confidence interval included 0.5, so the ranking is exploratory. No gene was differentially expressed between stage groups after false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction (smallest FDR = 0.057, CD44). A co-expression network built from training tumours identified REL, EP300 and ESR1 as the most connected genes, a property that reflects co-expression rather than regulation or association with stage. Limitations include a single cohort, no external validation, no clinical covariates and a small number of late-stage test tumours. Expression of this gene panel carries limited but measurable information about anatomical stage; expression-based stage models should be combined with clinicopathological variables and validated in independent cohorts before any clinical application is considered.

items.title: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of the Patient-Artificial Intelligence Rating Instrument
items.abstract_or_text: Importance: Patients increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) for health-related conversations, but evaluation measures largely reflect clinician judgment. Objective: To develop and preliminarily evaluate a patient instrument assessing the quality of patient-AI health conversations. Design: Cross-sectional survey conducted June 5-14, 2026, following patient-partnered instrument development and cognitive interviews. Setting: An anonymous online survey. Participants: A convenience sample of adults with prior use of large language models for personal health-related queries, recruited from an academic medical center-affiliated Insight Panel and patient peers. Exposures: Participants' own prior health-related conversations with AI tools of their choosing. Main Outcomes and Measures: The Patient-AI Rating instrument comprised 12 communication-quality and patient engagement items rated from 1 to 5 and a separately scored patient-perceived-harm item. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach alpha, with sensitivity analyses using first ratings only for those using the tool to rate multiple conversations and participant-mean profiles. We examined item-total correlations, inter-item structure, and between- and within-participant variation. Results: Fourteen participants contributed 46 complete ratings; among 13 providing demographics, median age was 63 years (IQR, 53-70 years), and 8 (62%) reported female gender. Participants provided a median of 2 ratings (range, 1-17). Cronbach alpha was 0.88 (95% CI, 0.83-0.93) across all ratings, 0.85 using first ratings only, and 0.92 using participant-mean profiles. Corrected item-total correlations ranged from 0.42 to 0.72; mean inter-item correlation was 0.40. No item deletion improved Cronbach alpha. The mean quality score was 4.43 (SD, 0.45). Among 9 participants contributing multiple ratings, the intraclass correlation coefficient was 0.45, suggesting inter-conversation variability. No perceived harm was reported in 44 of 46 ratings (96%); the harm item correlated minimally with the instrument total (r = 0.09). Conclusions and Relevance: In this small cross-sectional study of engaged patients, the Patient-AI Rating instrument showed promising internal consistency and variation across rated conversations. These findings support further evaluation of patient-reported communication quality alongside clinician-based measures. Validation in larger, more diverse populations, including assessment of construct and criterion validity, is needed before broader use.

items.title: Pannexin-1 regulates cellular identity and excitability in the developing cortex
items.abstract_or_text: Mutations in genes encoding a range of ion-conducting proteins disrupt development of the cerebral cortex in humans, often causing polymicrogyria (PMG); yet how ion conduction guides the development of cortical architecture is not clear. Here, we describe three individuals with brain malformations including PMG and microcephaly in whom de novo, missense mutations were identified in PANX1--encoding an ATP and ion conducting channel. We show that these PMG-associated PANX1 mutations (p.D14H, p.M37R, and p.N338T) disrupt normal glycosylation and confer gain-of-function with respect to ATP release and channel conductance. In vivo modeling of mutant PANX1 in cortical progenitor cells demonstrated disrupted cell migration and excess cell death in both mice and ferret models. In vitro modeling of the p.N338T allele in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived neurons further revealed changes in neuronal morphology and increased excitability, and dysregulation of key transcription factors critical for neurogenesis and cell fate. In addition, p.N338T iPSC-derived neural progenitor cells displayed increased PANX1 activation. Our results show that normal PANX1 function contributes to cortical structure through regulation of ion conductance and ATP release and provides insight into how these processes influence corticogenesis and cytoarchitecture more broadly.

items.title: Dissociation between impaired explicit spatial remapping and preserved implicit neural dynamics in Alzheimers disease
items.abstract_or_text: The hippocampus supports spatial memory by dynamically integrating external sensory inputs with intrinsic neural circuit dynamics during novel experience. In Alzheimer's disease (AD), despite impaired hippocampal spatial remapping, learning and memory-related hippocampal representations can remain partially preserved, a phenomenon consistent with cognitive resilience (Gomez-Isla and Frosch 2022, Jia, Xu et al. 2025). However, the hippocampal ensemble coding patterns associated with these preserved memory abilities remain remains unclear. We hypothesize that intrinsic temporal structures of neuronal firing continue to facilitate the encoding of new spatial information. Using the AppNL-G-F rat model, we recorded hippocampal CA1 activity across multiple days during a familiar-novel context alternating task. We found a dissociation between impaired explicit spatial coding and preserved implicit temporal coding in the AD hippocampal network. Explicit spatial coding was impaired, as place cells showed weak discrimination between distinct contexts and failed to exhibit improvement across days. In contrast, implicit temporal coding exhibited experience-dependent refinement, with cofiring dynamic becoming increasingly context-specific across long-term experience. Further analysis suggested that the enhancement of implicit cofiring may be associated with the increased consistency of neural ensemble reactivation during sharp wave ripples in awake rest. Taken together, these findings reveal an explicit-implicit dissociation in the AD hippocampal network, suggesting that the experience-dependent refinement of implicit temporal coding may support preserved learning-related hippocampal network dynamics despite impaired spatial remapping.

items.title: Agent K: An Agent-Orchestrated Pipeline for Mapping Genes to Biosynthetic Pathway towards Metabolite Discovery
items.abstract_or_text: The identification of biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) and their associated metabolic path- ways is central to genome-guided natural product discovery. However, existing computational tools depend on fragmented workflows for data processing, annotation, and analysis, which re- quire substantial manual intervention and lack seamless integration across heterogeneous plat- forms and tools. Here, we present, Agent K, an agent-orchestrated framework that automates the end-to-end process from bacterial whole genome sequence analysis to biosynthetic pathway mapping and metabolite discovery as candidate gene products for functional insights. The sys- tem employs a large-language-model (LLM) agent to coordinate multiple bioinformatics tools, enabling dynamic execution, data integration, result interpretation, and flexible and intuitive visualization. By integrating genomic sequences to functional annotations and pathway-level reconstructions, the framework facilitates the identification of candidate gene products, their biosynthetic pathways associated with individual BGCs, and the putative metabolites produced by those pathways. The developed novel agentic framework provides a user-friendly scalable and extensible solution for automated high-throughput analysis and mapping of bacterial secondary metabolism pathways for interactive exploration of candidate potential.

items.title: Sex differences in quantitative fundus parameters measured by artificial intelligence: a cross-sectional community study
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Automated analysis of fundus photographs yields numerous quantitative measures, but sex differences in these measures and their modification by systemic conditions are not well characterized. We quantified these differences in a large community screening cohort. Methods This cross-sectional study included 21,844 participants contributing 32,576 eye-level records to a community health-screening program in Ganzhou, China. EVisionAI was used to quantify 49 vascular, optic disc and cup, peripapillary atrophy, and fundus tessellation density parameters from color fundus photographs. Generalized estimating equations clustered by participant estimated male-female differences in standardized parameters. Models were unadjusted, adjusted for age and age squared, and further adjusted for 20 binary systemic conditions. Sex-by-condition interactions were examined for 19 conditions; prostatic hyperplasia was assessed separately using a three-level variable. Benjamini–Hochberg correction was applied across all fundus parameters within each model for the primary comparisons and within each condition for the interaction analyses. Results Mean age was 63.6 ± 9.8 years in women and 63.9 ± 10.1 years in men. After full adjustment and FDR correction, sex differences were found in 41 of 49 parameters: 19 of 22 optic disc and cup, 8 of 11 vascular, 7 of 7 peripapillary atrophy, and 7 of 9 fundus tessellation density measures. The largest standardized differences in men were a lower disc vertical-to-horizontal ratio (β = −0.170; 95% confidence interval, − 0.196 to − 0.144) and a higher atrophy arc height-to-disc vertical diameter ratio (β = 0.166; 95% confidence interval, 0.141 to 0.192). The arteriole-to-venule ratio was also lower in men (β = −0.113; 95% confidence interval, − 0.137 to − 0.089). Estimates were generally stable across models. Twenty-three effect-modification findings remained significant after false discovery rate correction, predominantly involving prostatic hyperplasia. Conclusions Sex differences were present across most quantitative fundus parameters and changed little after adjustment for measured systemic conditions. Their relevance to screening requires validation in datasets with ocular biometry and clinical outcomes.

items.title: Diagnostic Loss: Asymmetric Supervision for Radiology Report Generation
items.abstract_or_text: Automated radiology report generation requires models to do more than produce fluent clinical narratives: they must explicitly state supported diagnoses while avoiding unsupported ones. However, existing medical vision-language models (MedVLMs) are typically trained with token-level maximum likelihood objectives, which prioritize text agreement over diagnostically critical terms. As a result, models can miss key diagnoses and introduce wrong ones. We identify this as an objective misalignment between conventional language modeling and the asymmetric diagnostic requirements of radiology reporting. To encode these requirements, we introduce Diagnostic Loss (DLoss), a differentiable, architecture-agnostic objective that operates directly on decoder token probabilities. DLoss separately aggregates probability mass over vocabularies associated with diagnoses supported by the reference report and with unsupported alternatives. Using asymmetric pooling across token positions in the report, it encourages supported diagnoses to receive sufficient probability in at least one position while suppressing spurious probability spikes for unsupported diagnoses across all positions during training. The loss can be applied to existing 3D MedVLMs without modifying their vision backbones, language decoders, or inference procedures, and introduces no additional inference-time computation. We train and evaluate DLoss on 50,000 abdominal CT scans across several 3D MedVLM architectures on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution report-generation benchmarks. Across these settings, DLoss improves diagnostic faithfulness while maintaining competitive performance on conventional language-generation metrics, showing the value of asymmetric sequence-level supervision for radiology report generation. The code for DLoss is available at https://github.com/gmum/DLoss.

items.title: TESSA: A Governance-Oriented Custom GPT for SME Guidance under the EU AI Act: Design, Implementation, and Evaluation
items.abstract_or_text: The increasing adoption of generative AI presents new opportunities while raising AI governance and regulatory challenges, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) navigating the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act). To support AI governance education, this study developed TESSA, a governance-oriented educational artifact within the OpenAI Custom GPT environment. Following a design science research approach, TESSA was evaluated against baseline ChatGPT using 100 benchmark scenarios through governance alignment assessment, human expert review, and consistency testing. Preliminary LLM-assisted assessment showed governance alignment rates of 90% for TESSA and 83% for baseline ChatGPT, while independent validation by an AI regulation law practitioner yielded 71% and 70%, respectively. Human expert review indicated that both systems provided generally strong governance guidance, while TESSA maintained high consistency across repeated executions. The findings suggest that governance-oriented grounding can support structured, practical, and stable AI-assisted compliance guidance for SMEs. The study contributes (i) a governance-oriented Custom GPT artifact for AI governance education, (ii) a human-validated regulatory update mechanism, and (iii) a multidimensional evaluation framework for governance-oriented AI artifact.

items.title: Probabilistic uncertainty in virtual spatial transcriptomics from histology is largely redundant with the predicted mean
items.abstract_or_text: Deep learning has enabled virtual spatial transcriptomics from histology, offering a scalable approach to molecular profiling of routinely archived tissue without molecular assays. However, reliable uncertainty estimates are essential for identifying potentially inaccurate predictions, and it remains unclear whether existing methods provide useful information about prediction reliability. Here, we present a systematic benchmark of uncertainty estimation for virtual spatial transcriptomics across three cancer cohorts spanning melanoma, lung, and kidney tumors. We evaluate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty using probabilistic likelihoods and approximate Bayesian methods alongside histology-free and training-free baselines, assessing both calibration and error informativeness. Across cohorts and methods, uncertainty is associated with prediction error, but the predicted mean largely explains this association. After accounting for the mean, uncertainty provides only weak information about larger errors. Moreover, good calibration does not imply informative uncertainty, with simple distributions fitted without histology achieving comparable calibration. We therefore distinguish calibrated from informative uncertainty and argue that uncertainty should provide information about prediction error beyond the predicted mean. This benchmark provides a framework for systematic uncertainty evaluation in virtual spatial transcriptomics. Code availability: https://github.com/ratschlab/uncertainty-vst-2026

items.title: Feasibility study on using the diffusion-weighted imaging liver pulsation artifact as marker of liver fibrosis
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Liver diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) often shows signal loss in the left lobe due to cardiac pulsation, known as the pulsation artifact. Purpose: This study was conducted to turn this bug into a feature. We hypothesized that the pulsation artifact, caused by mechanically transmitted waves, is influenced by tissue stiffness and, thereby, indicative of cirrhosis in the left liver lobe. Thus, we evaluated the potential of DWI pulsation artifacts to detect liver cirrhosis. Study type: This study included both retrospective patients and prospective healthy volunteers. Study population: Thirteen healthy volunteers, 16 patients with cirrhosis (Ishak 5 or 6), and three patients without cirrhosis (Ishak 0, 1, or 2) were included. Field Strength/Sequence: Imaging was performed at 1.5 T and 3 T using echoplanar DWI of the liver with two b-values, b50 = 50 s/mm2 and b800 = 800 s/mm2. Assessment: After manual segmentation of the left and right liver lobes, 18 first-order features were extracted from b50 and b800 images. We assumed the pulsation artifact was predominantly present in the left liver lobe in the b800 images. Thus, we computed the ratios of the intensity-normalized b800 features obtained from the left and right liver lobes. Additionally, we performed an intensity normalization to address the sometimes different signal intensities of left and right liver lobe. Then, we conducted a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis to differentiate cirrhotic from non- cirrhotic livers. Statistical tests: ROC analysis and leave-one-out bootstrapping were applied, both yielding area under the curve (AUC) values. Results: Left liver pulsation artifacts were more pronounced in non-cirrhotic livers and largely absent in cirrhotic livers. The first quartile feature, i.e. the first quartile of the normalized signal, best distinguished cirrhotic from non-cirrhotic livers (AUC = 0.95; 95% confidence interval 0.87-1.00). Data conclusion: The left liver DWI pulsation artifact reflects liver stiffness and could serve as a simple, intrinsic marker of liver cirrhosis. Analysis of the signal magnitude can differentiate cirrhotic from non-cirrhotic livers.

items.title: Reconstructing human gene regulatory evolution using deep learning
items.abstract_or_text: Understanding the genetic changes that drove the evolution of human-specific traits is a central goal in biology. Changes in gene expression are thought to be a major source of phenotypic innovations, but identifying the underlying changes in cis-regulatory elements (CREs) along the human lineage has been difficult: functional data from great apes are scarce and unobtainable for extinct hominins, and pinpointing causal substitutions requires knowing which sequences determine CRE activity. Here, we used AlphaGenome, a sequence-to-function deep-learning model, to predict the cis-regulatory effects of ~17 million single-nucleotide substitutions specific to the human lineage and traced their consequences for gene expression evolution across 305 tissues and cell types. The 71,345 predicted cis-regulatory gains lie mostly outside human accelerated regions and arose either through creation of new CREs or, more often, through co-option of CREs ancestrally accessible in other tissues. They are also enriched for distal enhancers and for target gene functions characteristic of the corresponding tissues, suggesting that they contributed to the evolution of tissue-specific biology in humans. Genes linked to more gains were more likely to be upregulated in humans, and in silico reversion to ancestral alleles traced such upregulations to individual substitutions creating transcription factor binding motifs. Comparison with Neandertal and Denisovan genomes revealed that nearly all gains now fixed in humans predate the split from archaic hominins, yet a few modern-human-specific gains contribute substantially to gene upregulation. Our study provides a genome-wide, tissue-resolved map of cis-regulatory changes and their contribution to gene expression evolution along the human lineage.
